findings.title: Double-clicking "Add task" saves 2 times
1 page shows an error when opened directly (a reload or a shared link breaks)
findings.meaning: Opening one of the app's own links directly, the way a reload or a shared link would, shows an error or a "page not found" view, even though the same link works when clicked inside the app.
findings.impact: Anyone who reloads the page, bookmarks it or opens a shared link lands on an error instead of the page they expected. Deep links and refreshes are broken.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "Opening these pages directly returns an error or a not-found view, though they work when navigated to inside the app. This is usually a single-page app served without a fallback to index.html: configure the host to serve index.html for any unknown path so the client router can handle it."

findings.title: Secret key shipped to every visitor: a Stripe secret key
3 security header problems (Content-Security-Policy, Clickjacking protection, X-Content-Type-Options)
Session cookie "fernway_session" has no HttpOnly
Account B can read Account A's data (1 endpoint)
findings.meaning: Signed in as Account B, Run Hound could read data that belongs to Account A from 1 endpoint. Two accounts that should not see each other's data are not kept apart by the server.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can read another user's private data (their records, their profile), so nothing a person keeps in this app is private from other accounts.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "These endpoints return one account's data to another signed-in account: GET /api/tasks. Check on the server that the signed-in user owns the record before returning it, and answer 403 or 404 otherwise."

findings.title: Account A's data is readable without signing in (3 endpoints)
A page on another site can change Account A's data (no CSRF protection)
findings.meaning: Run Hound opened a page on a different site (http://127.0.0.1:44383) in Account A's browser and sent POST /api/tasks again with a new value (form-encoded). Re-reading the record as Account A showed the new value: the browser attached Account A's cookie fernway_session (SameSite=None) to a request from another site, and the server accepted it with no CSRF token and no Origin check.
findings.impact: Any web page Account A visits could silently make this change (or any other this form makes) on their behalf, without them ever submitting the form. This is a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) flaw.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "The save at POST /api/tasks can be sent from another site. Add a CSRF defence: a SameSite=Lax (or Strict) session cookie, plus a per-request CSRF token the server checks, or an Origin/Referer check that rejects requests from other sites. Accept only application/json for JSON saves."

lines: > No CSRF token and no Origin check stopped it.

findings.title: Account B can change Account A's records
findings.meaning: Run Hound saved a test record as Account A, then sent PATCH /api/tasks/ffb60789-31bc-410f-8423-0a2247330054 as Account B. Re-reading the record as Account A showed it had changed (title). The server doesn't check that the record belongs to whoever sends the update.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can change other users' records by sending their ids (insecure direct object reference).
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "PATCH /api/tasks/ffb60789-31bc-410f-8423-0a2247330054 must only let the signed-in owner of the record change it: require a session, look the record up by id AND the session user's id, and answer 404 (or 403) otherwise. The same for every update and delete route."

findings.title: "Bio" is not saved
1 page shows an error when opened directly (a reload or a shared link breaks)
Secret key shipped to every visitor: a Stripe secret key
3 security header problems (Content-Security-Policy, Clickjacking protection, X-Content-Type-Options)
Session cookie "fernway_session" has no HttpOnly
Account B can read Account A's data (1 endpoint)
Account A's data is readable without signing in (1 endpoint)
The server accepted admin fields the form never sends: role, isAdmin, is_admin and admin (mass assignment)
findings.meaning: Run Hound added role, isAdmin, is_admin and admin to the form's own save, and the server stored them. The form never offers these fields, but the server takes whatever the browser sends. Anyone can make themselves an admin by adding one field to a request.
findings.impact: A normal user can give themselves admin rights, or any other role, by editing the save request in their browser. This is one of the most serious flaws an app can have.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "The save at PUT /api/users/alex-rivera/profile accepts role, isAdmin, is_admin and admin from the browser. On the server, accept only the fields the form is meant to change and ignore everything else (an allow-list), so role and admin flags can never be set by the client."

findings.title: Account A got a paid plan without paying
findings.meaning: Run Hound opened /app/upgraded as Account A, on the free plan and without paying anything, and let the page run as it would for any visitor. Reading Account A's plan again as Account A (GET /api/users/alex-rivera/profile) afterwards showed plan "free" → "pro": the server changed it because a success page was loaded, not because a payment was confirmed.
findings.impact: Anyone with a free account can get the paid plan (or its credits) for nothing, just by opening this address. You lose the revenue, and paid features are open to everyone who finds it.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "Opening /app/upgraded upgrades the signed-in account without a payment: the server trusts the success page. Grant a plan only from a verified payment: the payment provider's webhook (for example Stripe's checkout.session.completed, checked with its signing secret), or a server-side lookup of the checkout session by its id that checks it was paid, by this account, and wasn't used before. The success page should only show the result."
